title: Miller I: Article 50
fact: The Supreme Court ruled that ministers could not trigger Article 50 using prerogative powers alone; an Act of Parliament was needed.
analysis: Parliamentary sovereignty limits executive prerogative where domestic legal rights would change.
counter: The ruling did not prevent Brexit; Parliament subsequently authorised notification.
uses: Sovereignty; rule of law; judicial independence

title: Miller II: prorogation
fact: The Supreme Court held Boris Johnson's advice to prorogue Parliament unlawful because it frustrated parliamentary accountability without reasonable justification.
analysis: The uncodified constitution can generate enforceable limits on executive power.
counter: Critics argue courts entered a politically sensitive area; supporters distinguish legal limits from political merits.
uses: Separation of powers; constitution; PM power

title: Human Rights Act
fact: The Act gives domestic effect to most ECHR rights and allows courts to issue declarations of incompatibility for primary legislation.
analysis: Balances rights protection with Parliament's formal legislative supremacy.
counter: A declaration does not itself strike down an Act of Parliament.

title: Constitutional Reform Act
fact: The Act reformed the Lord Chancellor's role, established a UK Supreme Court that opened in 2009, and supported a more visible separation of powers.
analysis: Strengthened institutional judicial independence and transparency.
counter: The UK still retains significant overlap between executive and legislature.

title: European Union (Withdrawal) Act
fact: The Act provided for repeal of the European Communities Act 1972 on exit and conversion of much EU-derived law into domestic law.
analysis: Demonstrates Parliament's capacity to reshape constitutional relationships through statute.
counter: Continuity of retained law shows sovereignty does not imply instant policy autonomy.

title: Brexit withdrawal agreement defeats
fact: Theresa May's withdrawal agreement was defeated in the Commons three times, including by 230 votes in January.
analysis: Even a governing party can lose control when backbenchers and opposition coordinate.
counter: Unusual party divisions make it a poor example of routine government-Parliament relations.

title: Lords and tax credits
fact: The House of Lords voted to delay government tax-credit regulations, triggering a debate about the Lords' powers and the Strathclyde Review.
analysis: An unelected second chamber can check secondary legislation.
counter: The Lords' democratic legitimacy is contested and conventions constrain its role.

title: Privileges Committee and Johnson
fact: The Commons Privileges Committee concluded that Boris Johnson had deliberately misled the House over statements about gatherings; he disputed its conclusions and resigned as an MP.
analysis: Committees can investigate and enforce standards even against senior political figures.
counter: Political polarisation can shape public reception of committee findings.

title: Fixed-term Parliaments Act repeal
fact: The Dissolution and Calling of Parliament Act repealed the 2011 fixed-term election framework.
analysis: Shows constitutional statutes can be reversed through ordinary legislation.
counter: Debate remains over whether restored dissolution powers favour incumbents.

title: Poll tax
fact: The Community Charge became politically unpopular and contributed to pressure on Margaret Thatcher's leadership.
analysis: A powerful PM can still be constrained by party dissent and public opinion.
counter: Leadership change had multiple causes including Europe and cabinet relations.

title: Iraq War decision
fact: Tony Blair's government joined the US-led invasion of Iraq; the Chilcot Inquiry reported in 2016 and criticised aspects of decision-making.
analysis: Strong parliamentary majorities and executive information advantages can concentrate foreign-policy power.
counter: Parliament held a Commons vote in 2003 and later scrutiny exposed weaknesses.

title: Truss mini-budget
fact: The September fiscal statement prompted severe market turbulence and political backlash; Liz Truss resigned after 49 days in office.
analysis: Financial markets, party confidence and cabinet cohesion can sharply constrain PM autonomy.
counter: It was an exceptional episode, not a normal limit on every government.

title: Cameron and EU referendum
fact: David Cameron called a referendum on EU membership; Leave won 51.9% to 48.1%, and Cameron resigned.
analysis: A PM's use of direct democracy can transform the constitutional agenda and undermine their own authority.
counter: Referendums can also be defended as a legitimate democratic mandate.

title: UNISON tribunal fees
fact: The Supreme Court quashed employment tribunal fees introduced by secondary legislation because they obstructed access to justice.
analysis: Judicial review can protect practical rights against executive action.
counter: Judges did not invalidate primary legislation.
uses: Rule of law; rights; judicial review

title: Belmarsh detention case
fact: The Law Lords issued a declaration of incompatibility concerning indefinite detention of certain foreign terror suspects.
analysis: Rights review can exert political pressure on ministers and Parliament.
counter: The declaration did not automatically nullify the legislation.

title: Rwanda asylum policy judgment
fact: The Supreme Court held the then government's Rwanda removals policy unlawful on the evidence before it because of risks of refoulement.
analysis: Courts can review executive policy against domestic legal obligations.
counter: Parliament later legislated on the issue, highlighting institutional conflict.

title: Scottish independence referendum
fact: Scotland voted 55.3% No and 44.7% Yes in an agreed referendum.
analysis: Devolution can coexist with strong constitutional demands for self-determination.
counter: The vote maintained the Union and showed the independence movement was not universally supported.

title: Scottish Continuity Bill case
fact: The Supreme Court considered competence of Scottish legislation in relation to EU withdrawal and subsequent UK legislation.
analysis: The UK Parliament remains legally sovereign over devolved competences.
counter: Political conventions and legitimacy complicate purely legal accounts.

title: Northern Ireland power sharing
fact: The Good Friday Agreement established a framework for devolved power-sharing and consent principles.
analysis: Devolution can support conflict resolution through institutional inclusion.
counter: Executive suspensions illustrate how fragile power-sharing can be.

title: Representation of the People Act
fact: The Act enfranchised most men aged 21 and over and some women aged 30 and over who met property qualifications.
analysis: Democracy expanded through sustained social mobilisation and reform.
counter: Full equal voting ages for women and men came in 1928.

title: Suffragettes and suffragists
fact: The WSPU used militant tactics while the NUWSS emphasised constitutional campaigning for women's suffrage.
analysis: Different strategies can pressure political institutions toward reform.
counter: Historians debate their relative impact alongside war and wider social change.

title: 2016 referendum turnout
fact: EU referendum turnout was 72.2%, higher than the 2015 general election turnout of 66.1%.
analysis: High-salience direct democracy can mobilise participation.
counter: A single vote does not establish informed deliberation or sustained engagement.

title: 1979 general election
fact: Margaret Thatcher's Conservatives won a Commons majority amid economic dissatisfaction and industrial conflict.
analysis: Leadership, economic context and party reputation can drive electoral change.
counter: Electoral outcomes also reflect the voting system and long-term social shifts.

title: 1997 general election
fact: Tony Blair's Labour won 418 seats with 43.2% of the UK vote, ending 18 years of Conservative government.
analysis: Campaign repositioning, leadership and the FPTP seat bonus shaped a landslide.
counter: The result also reflected Conservative division and voter fatigue.

title: 2019 general election
fact: Conservatives won 365 seats on 43.6% of the vote; Labour won 202 seats.
analysis: Brexit alignment, leadership and constituency geography helped shape a decisive seat outcome.
counter: National vote shares alone cannot explain constituency-level swings.

title: 2024 general election
fact: Labour won 411 seats on about 33.7% of votes; Reform UK won around 14.3% but five seats.
analysis: A dramatic illustration of disproportionality under FPTP and geographically concentrated support.
counter: FPTP supporters argue it can facilitate decisive government and local representation.

title: 2011 AV referendum
fact: Voters rejected replacing FPTP with the Alternative Vote by 67.9% to 32.1%.
analysis: Electoral reform requires more than dissatisfaction with FPTP.
counter: AV is not a proportional system; the vote does not settle all PR proposals.

title: 2010 Conservative–Lib Dem coalition
fact: No party won a Commons majority; Conservatives and Liberal Democrats formed a coalition government.
analysis: Coalition government challenges the idea FPTP always produces single-party majorities.
counter: It was unusual in postwar UK politics.

title: Labour Clause IV revision
fact: Labour revised Clause IV, moving away from an explicit commitment to common ownership of the means of production.
analysis: Party ideology can evolve to appeal to a wider electorate.
counter: Critics see ideological dilution; supporters see electoral adaptation.

title: UKIP and Brexit agenda
fact: UKIP won the largest UK share of votes in the 2014 European Parliament election, influencing debate about EU membership.
analysis: Smaller parties can shape agendas without winning many Westminster seats.
counter: Their impact depends on media attention and major-party responses.

title: British Medical Association
fact: The BMA organised junior doctor industrial action during a dispute over contracts in England.
analysis: Professional groups can combine expertise, membership and collective action.
counter: Access and influence do not guarantee policy victory.

title: Extinction Rebellion protests
fact: XR organised disruptive climate protests, drawing attention to climate policy and protest rights.
analysis: Outsider groups can gain visibility and shift the agenda.
counter: Disruption may alienate some voters and influence is difficult to measure.

title: Marcus Rashford school meals campaign
fact: Campaigning helped prompt changes to government provision of support for children during school holidays.
analysis: Public figures and civil society can influence policy outside elections.
counter: It is difficult to separate campaigning effects from wider political pressures.

title: European Communities Act
fact: The Act gave effect to the UK's entry into the European Communities and provided a route for EU law in domestic law.
analysis: Illustrates a major statutory transformation of the UK constitutional order.
counter: Parliament retained legal capacity to repeal the Act, which it later did.

title: Brexit referendum and exit
fact: The 2016 Leave vote preceded UK withdrawal from the EU on 31 January 2020.
analysis: EU membership can reshape parties, elections and debates about sovereignty.
counter: Formal withdrawal did not end economic and regulatory interdependence.

title: Marbury v Madison
fact: The US Supreme Court established judicial review of federal legislation as a central constitutional practice.
analysis: Judicial review enables courts to check Congress and the executive.
counter: Judicial supremacy raises democratic legitimacy questions.

title: US constitutional amendments
fact: Article V sets a demanding amendment process requiring supermajorities at federal and state level; 27 amendments have been ratified.
analysis: Entrenchment protects stability and fundamental rules.
counter: High barriers can obstruct reforms with substantial public support.

title: National Federation of Independent Business v Sebelius
fact: The Supreme Court upheld the Affordable Care Act's individual mandate as a tax while limiting federal leverage over states through Medicaid expansion.
analysis: Federalism creates legal constraints on federal policy design.
counter: Congress retains substantial taxation and spending powers.

title: 2018–2019 federal shutdown
fact: A funding dispute over border-wall appropriations led to a 35-day partial federal government shutdown.
analysis: Separate elected branches can produce gridlock over spending.
counter: Budget bargaining can also be viewed as genuine legislative leverage.

title: Trump first impeachment
fact: The House impeached Donald Trump in 2019; the Senate acquitted him in February 2020.
analysis: Impeachment gives Congress a constitutional mechanism to hold presidents accountable.
counter: Partisanship and the two-thirds conviction threshold limit removal.

title: January 6 committee
fact: A House select committee investigated the January 6 attack on the Capitol and published findings.
analysis: Committees can gather evidence and scrutinise threats to constitutional processes.
counter: Committees lack judicial power and their political influence can be contested.

title: Filibuster and cloture
fact: Most Senate legislation can face extended debate; under current rules cloture generally needs 60 votes, with important exceptions.
analysis: Minority obstruction can frustrate a simple majority.
counter: Supporters argue it encourages bargaining and protects minority voices.

title: Youngstown Sheet & Tube v Sawyer
fact: The Supreme Court rejected President Truman's seizure of steel mills during the Korean War.
analysis: Emergency claims do not automatically create domestic executive authority.
counter: Presidential powers vary depending on congressional authorisation.

title: United States v Nixon
fact: The Supreme Court required President Nixon to comply with a subpoena for Watergate tapes, rejecting absolute executive privilege.
analysis: Courts can constrain presidential secrecy and reinforce the rule of law.
counter: Executive privilege remains recognised in qualified form.

title: Obama and DACA
fact: The Obama administration created Deferred Action for Childhood Arrivals through executive immigration enforcement discretion.
analysis: Presidents can influence policy when Congress is gridlocked.
counter: Executive actions are vulnerable to legal challenge and later administrations.

title: Trump v United States
fact: The Supreme Court recognised presidential immunity for official acts, with absolute immunity for core constitutional powers and presumptive immunity for other official acts.
analysis: Raises the stakes of debates over presidential accountability and separation of powers.
counter: The decision did not declare blanket immunity for unofficial conduct.
uses: Executive; Supreme Court; rule of law

title: Brown v Board of Education
fact: The Supreme Court held state-sponsored racial segregation in public schools unconstitutional.
analysis: Courts can catalyse major civil-rights change through constitutional interpretation.
counter: Implementation required political mobilisation and federal enforcement.

title: Dobbs v Jackson
fact: The Supreme Court overruled Roe v Wade, holding the federal Constitution does not confer a right to abortion.
analysis: Judicial appointments and interpretation can reshape rights policy across states.
counter: The ruling returned broad policy authority to elected institutions, but rights protections vary.

title: Obergefell v Hodges
fact: The Supreme Court recognised a constitutional right to same-sex marriage nationwide.
analysis: Judicial interpretation can expand equal protection and liberty guarantees.
counter: Critics question courts settling disputed social policy; supporters stress minority rights.

title: Citizens United v FEC
fact: The Supreme Court held restrictions on independent political spending by corporations and unions unconstitutional under the First Amendment.
analysis: Free speech doctrine strongly shapes US campaign finance.
counter: Independent spending is legally distinct from direct candidate contributions.

title: 2000 Bush v Gore
fact: The Supreme Court halted the Florida recount in the closely contested presidential election; George W Bush won the Electoral College.
analysis: Electoral rules and judicial decisions can affect presidential legitimacy.
counter: The ruling was explicitly limited in its application and the popular vote is not decisive under the system.

title: 2016 presidential election
fact: Donald Trump won the Electoral College while Hillary Clinton won the national popular vote.
analysis: The Electoral College can diverge from the popular vote and prioritises state geography.
counter: Defenders argue it reinforces the federal nature of presidential elections.

title: 2020 presidential election
fact: Joe Biden won 306 electoral votes to Donald Trump's 232; courts rejected numerous challenges to the outcome.
analysis: Election administration and institutional checks are central to legitimacy.
counter: Political distrust can persist despite formal certification.

title: 2022 midterm elections
fact: Republicans won a narrow House majority while Democrats retained control of the Senate.
analysis: Different election cycles and constituency patterns shape divided government.
counter: Midterms are not a simple referendum on presidential popularity.

title: NRA and gun policy
fact: The National Rifle Association has historically mobilised members and lobbied around Second Amendment interpretation and legislation.
analysis: Organised interests can influence agenda-setting and legislative incentives.
counter: Its influence varies by election, funding, public opinion and policy context.

title: Super PACs after SpeechNow
fact: Following Citizens United and SpeechNow.org v FEC, independent-expenditure-only committees could raise unlimited funds subject to independence rules.
analysis: Campaign finance allows well-funded interests significant visibility.
counter: Disclosure requirements and the distinction between independent spending and coordination still matter.

title: Civil Rights Act
fact: Federal law prohibited discrimination in major areas including public accommodations and employment.
analysis: Congressional legislation can transform civil-rights enforcement.
counter: Legal equality does not automatically eliminate social and economic inequalities.

title: Voting Rights Act
fact: The Act targeted discriminatory voting practices, including federal oversight mechanisms later altered by Supreme Court decisions.
analysis: Federal intervention can safeguard participation where states discriminate.
counter: Debates continue about the appropriate scope of federal election oversight.

title: Shelby County v Holder
fact: The Supreme Court invalidated the Voting Rights Act coverage formula for preclearance, rendering that mechanism inoperative without new legislation.
analysis: Judicial rulings can narrow federal voting-rights enforcement.
counter: The Court did not strike down the entire Voting Rights Act.

title: UK versus US constitutional rigidity
fact: UK Parliament can generally amend constitutional rules by ordinary Acts; US constitutional amendments face Article V hurdles.
analysis: Structural comparison: flexibility versus entrenched higher law.
counter: UK constitutional change can still be politically and legally complex.

title: PM versus president
fact: A UK PM normally depends on Commons confidence and party leadership; a US president has a separately elected fixed term.
analysis: Structural incentives create different forms of executive-legislative accountability.
counter: Party unity, personality and crises modify formal powers.

title: UKSC versus SCOTUS
fact: UK courts cannot normally strike down Acts of Parliament; US courts can invalidate legislation conflicting with the Constitution.
analysis: Different sources of sovereignty explain differences in judicial authority.
counter: Both courts can substantially influence executive policy and rights.

title: FPTP and Electoral College
fact: UK Commons seats are elected in single-member constituencies; US presidential elections use state-based Electoral College allocations.
analysis: Institutions mediate popular preferences in different ways.
counter: Both systems interact with party geography and turnout, not just formal rules.

title: John Locke and natural rights
fact: Locke argued political authority rests on consent and should protect life, liberty and property.
analysis: Supports limited government and the legitimacy of resistance to arbitrary power.
counter: Critics question unequal property relations and the practical boundaries of consent.

title: J S Mill and harm principle
fact: Mill defended extensive liberty of thought and action unless conduct harms others.
analysis: Individuality and experimentation are central to liberal development.
counter: Defining harm and distinguishing self-regarding acts is contested.

title: John Rawls and original position
fact: Rawls used the veil of ignorance to justify equal basic liberties and inequalities arranged to benefit the least advantaged.
analysis: Provides a modern liberal case for redistribution and fairness.
counter: Libertarians dispute redistributive obligations and entitlement principles.

title: T H Green and positive freedom
fact: Green argued freedom requires conditions for self-development, not merely absence of interference.
analysis: Explains why modern liberals support enabling social policies.
counter: State intervention may itself restrict negative liberty.

title: Mary Wollstonecraft and equality
fact: Wollstonecraft argued women's apparent inferiority reflected unequal education and opportunity, not natural incapacity.
analysis: Universal liberal rights challenge inherited hierarchies.
counter: Formal rights may be insufficient without material and cultural change.

title: Betty Friedan and the feminine mystique
fact: Friedan criticised restrictive expectations of domestic femininity and helped inspire second-wave feminism.
analysis: Liberal reform can challenge exclusion in education and employment.
counter: Critics say early mainstream feminism often neglected differences of race and class.

title: Thomas Hobbes and security
fact: Hobbes argued that without effective authority, insecurity undermines peaceful social life.
analysis: Conservative arguments for order stress pessimism about conflict and human nature.
counter: His sovereign is more absolute than many later constitutional conservatives accept.

title: Edmund Burke and tradition
fact: Burke criticised abstract revolutionary reconstruction and defended gradual change informed by inherited institutions.
analysis: Tradition can embody accumulated social knowledge and practical wisdom.
counter: Inherited institutions can also preserve injustice.

title: Michael Oakeshott and scepticism
fact: Oakeshott contrasted practical political judgement with ambitious rationalist blueprints.
analysis: Supports pragmatic, limited political reform.
counter: Critics say scepticism can excuse avoidable inequality.

title: Ayn Rand and individualism
fact: Rand's objectivism defended rational self-interest and criticised collectivism.
analysis: Illustrates individualist arguments within the New Right.
counter: Her radical individualism conflicts with paternalist conservative traditions.

title: Robert Nozick and minimal state
fact: Nozick defended a minimal state and entitlement-based justice, opposing patterned redistribution.
analysis: Property rights and voluntary exchange can justify unequal outcomes.
counter: Critics challenge the justice of original holdings and historical inequalities.

title: Marx and Engels class conflict
fact: Marx and Engels presented history as shaped by class struggle and capitalist relations of production.
analysis: Links exploitation to economic structures rather than individual failure.
counter: Predictions about revolution and class polarisation remain disputed.

title: Rosa Luxemburg and mass strike
fact: Luxemburg stressed mass participation and spontaneous working-class action in revolutionary struggle.
analysis: Challenges overly centralised party leadership.
counter: Critics argue spontaneity alone may not secure durable change.

title: Beatrice Webb and gradual reform
fact: Webb championed cooperative and institutional routes to social improvement, associated with Fabian gradualism.
analysis: Demonstrates reformist and collective approaches within socialism.
counter: Critics see bureaucracy and elitism as risks.

title: Anthony Crosland and revisionism
fact: Crosland argued equality and welfare mattered more than nationalisation as an end in itself.
analysis: Social democracy can work within a mixed economy.
counter: Critics question whether capitalism permits deep equality.

title: Anthony Giddens and Third Way
fact: Giddens advocated modernised centre-left politics combining markets, social investment and responsibility.
analysis: Explains a shift away from traditional state ownership.
counter: Critics argue it accepts too many neoliberal assumptions.

title: Rousseau and general will
fact: Rousseau located legitimate sovereignty in the collective general will of citizens.
analysis: Links popular sovereignty to democratic national self-government.
counter: Claims to speak for a general will can suppress dissent.

title: Herder and cultural nationhood
fact: Herder emphasised shared language and cultural tradition in collective identity.
analysis: Cultural nationhood need not be defined solely by the state.
counter: Culture is plural and changes over time.

title: Mazzini and national self-determination
fact: Mazzini combined nationalism with republicanism and national liberation.
analysis: National movements can seek freedom and democratic government.
counter: National claims may conflict when populations overlap.

title: Marcus Garvey and pan-Africanism
fact: Garvey advocated Black self-determination, organisation and economic empowerment through pan-African ideas.
analysis: Nationalism can challenge imperial domination.
counter: His programme attracted criticism over strategy and essentialist elements.

title: Charles Maurras and integral nationalism
fact: Maurras promoted authoritarian, exclusionary integral nationalism and rejected democratic pluralism.
analysis: Shows nationalism can take illiberal and anti-democratic forms.
counter: Not all nationalisms share these exclusionary principles.

title: Charlotte Perkins Gilman and economics
fact: Gilman argued economic dependence entrenched gender inequality.
analysis: Connects social roles to material power and opportunity.
counter: Her wider writings contain views that require critical historical scrutiny.

title: Simone de Beauvoir and gender
fact: De Beauvoir argued femininity is shaped by social experience rather than fixed destiny.
analysis: Challenges essentialist accounts of gender roles.
counter: Debates continue about the relation of biology, identity and socialisation.

title: Kate Millett and sexual politics
fact: Millett analysed patriarchy as a political power relationship reproduced through culture and institutions.
analysis: Expands politics beyond formal government into private life.
counter: Critics dispute whether patriarchy explains all gender inequalities equally.

title: Sheila Rowbotham and socialist feminism
fact: Rowbotham linked women's oppression to class structures and capitalism.
analysis: Suggests economic and gender hierarchies reinforce one another.
counter: Critics argue class analysis can overlook other dimensions of identity.

title: bell hooks and intersectionality
fact: hooks challenged feminism that centred the experiences of privileged women and emphasised race, class and gender together.
analysis: Broadens equality analysis beyond a single category.
counter: Different feminist approaches dispute how best to prioritise reform.

title: Isaiah Berlin and plural values
fact: Berlin argued that important human values can conflict without a single perfect solution.
analysis: Supports tolerance and recognition of plural ways of life.
counter: Pluralism can complicate shared civic rules.

title: Will Kymlicka and minority rights
fact: Kymlicka defended group-differentiated rights in liberal democracies under conditions protecting individual liberty.
analysis: Cultural membership can support meaningful autonomy.
counter: Group rights can conflict with internal dissenters.

title: Charles Taylor and recognition
fact: Taylor argued identity and dignity are shaped by recognition from others.
analysis: Misrecognition can be a political injustice.
counter: Critics fear official recognition may entrench group boundaries.

title: Tariq Modood and civic multiculturalism
fact: Modood defended public recognition and accommodation of minority identities within shared citizenship.
analysis: Integration need not require assimilation.
counter: Debate persists over common values and institutional accommodation.

title: Bikhu Parekh and cultural dialogue
fact: Parekh argued societies should engage in intercultural dialogue about shared political principles.
analysis: Encourages mutual criticism and negotiation rather than rigid assimilation.
counter: Consensus can be difficult where values fundamentally conflict.

title: Max Stirner and the individual
fact: Stirner criticised imposed abstractions and defended radical individual autonomy.
analysis: Challenges authority claimed in the name of state or society.
counter: Critics question how stable cooperation emerges.

title: Bakunin and anti-statism
fact: Bakunin opposed authoritarian state power and argued for collective emancipation.
analysis: Highlights conflict between revolutionary freedom and centralised authority.
counter: Coordination without coercive institutions is challenging.

title: Emma Goldman and freedom
fact: Goldman defended personal freedom and criticised oppressive social and political hierarchies.
analysis: Anarchism extends liberty beyond voting to everyday relationships.
counter: Tensions exist between radical protest and wider public support.

title: Kropotkin and mutual aid
fact: Kropotkin argued cooperation is an important factor in evolution and social life.
analysis: Offers an optimistic account of human nature and voluntary solidarity.
counter: Critics question how voluntary arrangements scale to complex societies.

title: Proudhon and property
fact: Proudhon criticised exploitative property relations and advocated mutualist cooperation.
analysis: Separates possession and use from unequal ownership power.
counter: His property claims require careful distinctions and historical context.

title: Aldo Leopold and land ethic
fact: Leopold proposed extending ethical concern to ecological communities.
analysis: Nature may have moral significance beyond immediate human utility.
counter: Policy trade-offs remain between ecological protection and human needs.

title: Rachel Carson and Silent Spring
fact: Carson documented ecological concerns about pesticide use and stimulated environmental debate.
analysis: Scientific evidence can reshape environmental politics.
counter: Regulation requires evaluating specific risks and benefits.

title: E F Schumacher and small scale
fact: Schumacher advocated human-scale economics and appropriate technology.
analysis: Questions growth models focused solely on output.
counter: Small-scale solutions may struggle with large infrastructure needs.

title: Carolyn Merchant and ecofeminism
fact: Merchant examined links between attitudes toward nature, science and gender.
analysis: Connects environmental domination to wider power structures.
counter: Historical and philosophical claims are contested.

title: Murray Bookchin and social ecology
fact: Bookchin linked ecological damage to hierarchy and argued for decentralised democratic communities.
analysis: Environmental reform may require changing political power, not only technology.
counter: Local democracy alone may not solve global collective-action problems.

title: Duverger's law
fact: Single-member plurality elections tend to favour two large parties through mechanical and psychological effects.
analysis: Useful for analysing FPTP, strategic voting and party systems.
counter: It is a tendency rather than a universal rule; UK regional parties complicate it.

title: Median voter theorem
fact: Under restrictive assumptions, two vote-seeking parties converge toward the median voter.
analysis: Explains centrist manifesto incentives.
counter: Multi-dimensional preferences, turnout and primaries complicate the model.

title: Overton window
fact: The Overton window describes the range of policies viewed as politically acceptable at a given time.
analysis: Movements and events can change the perceived range of options.
counter: It is a descriptive metaphor, not a precise predictive law.

title: Robert Dahl and polyarchy
fact: Dahl described democracy through contestation and inclusive participation.
analysis: Helps distinguish real democratic competition from simple elections.
counter: Institutional procedures do not ensure equal influence.

title: Mancur Olson and collective action
fact: Olson analysed why large groups may struggle to organise despite shared interests.
analysis: Explains why concentrated interests can wield disproportionate influence.
counter: Identity and social norms can overcome free-rider problems.

title: Realism and balance of power
fact: Realists emphasise security, state interests and competition under international anarchy.
analysis: Provides a lens for alliance behaviour and deterrence.
counter: Can understate institutions, domestic politics and ethical commitments.

title: Liberal institutionalism
fact: Institutionalists argue international rules and organisations can facilitate cooperation.
analysis: Helps explain diplomacy and the role of the UN and EU.
counter: Institutions often depend on powerful states for enforcement.

title: Keynesian fiscal stimulus
fact: Keynesian theory argues public spending can support demand during downturns.
analysis: Connects economic policy to ideological debates over state intervention.
counter: Inflation, debt and supply constraints complicate application.

title: Public choice theory
fact: Public choice applies incentive-based analysis to politicians, voters and bureaucrats.
analysis: Challenges assumptions that state actors always maximise public welfare.
counter: It can understate public-service motivations and norms.

title: Gramsci and cultural hegemony
fact: Gramsci argued dominant ideas and institutions can help sustain social power.
analysis: Explains why political influence operates through culture and consent.
counter: Hard to isolate empirically from other causes of political stability.

title: Habermas and public sphere
fact: Habermas examined how public debate can legitimise democratic decision-making.
analysis: Highlights deliberation, media access and informed participation.
counter: Ideal deliberation is limited by inequality and misinformation.

title: UN right to food framework
fact: The Universal Declaration of Human Rights includes adequate living standards; Article 11 of the ICESCR recognises the right to adequate food.
analysis: Links social rights, institutions and the state’s positive obligations.
counter: Legal recognition alone does not guarantee implementation or funding.
